pages.text: The Sun

image.note: Cover: the blazing Sun above the earth

pages.text: Contents. Our Star / A Giant Ball of Fire / The Sun and the Earth / The Sun's Family / The Sun and Life / Living with the Sun.

Every morning it rises, and the world wakes. Every evening it sets, and the world sleeps. It gives us light, and warmth, and the very seasons of the year. Almost everything that lives depends upon it, and yet we hardly ever give it a thought. This is the story of the Sun, the ordinary star that means everything to us.

image.note: The Sun rising over a waking landscape

pages.text: The Sun looks small, a bright coin in the sky, but that is only because it is so far away. In truth it is a giant, so vast that more than a million earths could fit inside it. It is the largest thing in our whole corner of space, and everything near it, including us, dances to its tune.

image.note: The Sun's true size beside the tiny earth

pages.text: The Sun is a star, the same kind of blazing ball of gas as the tiny points you see at night. It seems so different from them only because it is so near. The other stars are suns far away; the Sun is a star close by. It is, quite simply, our own personal star.

image.note: The Sun beside distant stars, shown as the same

pages.text: And we are lucky to have it just where it is. If the Sun were much closer, our world would burn. Much further, and it would freeze. But at just the right distance, it warms the earth to exactly the temperature where water can flow and life can thrive. Our world sits, by great good fortune, in the Sun's warm and gentle glow.

image.note: The earth at just the right distance from the Sun

pages.text: The Sun is not solid. You could not stand on it, for it is a vast ball of glowing gas, so hot that nothing solid could survive there for an instant. Its surface blazes at thousands of degrees, and its heart is hotter still, hotter than anything you could ever imagine.

image.note: The Sun as a churning ball of glowing gas

pages.text: Deep in its core, the Sun makes its own energy, not by burning like a bonfire, but by a far more powerful process that crushes tiny parts of gas together and releases tremendous light and heat. It has been doing this for billions of years, and has enough fuel to keep going for billions more.

image.note: The blazing core of the Sun making energy

pages.text: All that light and heat pours out of the Sun in every direction, racing across space. A small part of it falls upon the earth, having crossed millions of kilometres in about eight minutes, and that small part is enough to light our days, warm our world, and feed nearly every living thing.

image.note: Light and heat streaming from the Sun to the earth

pages.text: The Sun gives us day and night, though not in the way you might think. The Sun does not travel round the earth. It only seems to, because the earth is turning. As our world spins, your part of it turns to face the Sun, and it is day; then it turns away, and it is night.

image.note: The spinning earth, one side lit, one side dark

pages.text: The Sun gives us the seasons too. The earth is tilted, just a little, as it circles the Sun. For part of the year your half of the world leans towards the Sun, and the days are long and warm. For another part it leans away, and the days are short and cool. That tilt is the reason for summer and winter.

image.note: The tilted earth circling the Sun through the seasons

pages.text: The Sun even makes the weather. Its heat lifts water from the seas into the sky, where it forms clouds and falls again as rain. Its warmth stirs the winds that sweep across the world. Almost every drop of rain and gust of wind begins, in the end, with the heat of the Sun.

image.note: The Sun lifting water, forming clouds and rain

pages.text: The Sun does not sit alone. It is circled by a family of worlds, the planets, held in their great loops by the Sun's mighty pull. The earth is one of them, one of eight, each a different size and distance, all of them wheeling endlessly around the same blazing star.

image.note: The Sun with its family of planets orbiting

pages.text: We call this family the Solar System, and the Sun is its heart and its ruler. Without the Sun's pull, the planets would drift away into the dark. Without its light, they would be frozen and lifeless. Every world in our neighbourhood belongs to the Sun, and follows it faithfully through space.

image.note: The Solar System, the Sun at its centre

pages.text: Here is the most important thing of all. Almost every living thing on earth is fed, in the end, by the Sun. Plants catch its light and turn it into food, growing green in its warmth. Animals eat the plants. Other animals eat those animals. And so the Sun's energy flows through every living thing.

image.note: Sunlight feeding a plant, then a chain of animals

pages.text: Even the food on your own plate is sunlight, in the end. The grain, the fruit, the vegetables grew in the Sun. The meat and milk came from animals that ate plants grown in the Sun. When you eat, you are eating captured sunshine. When you run and play, you are burning the Sun's energy, caught and stored by living things.

image.note: A meal traced back to sunlight and growing plants

pages.text: The Sun gives us life, but it is powerful, and must be treated with care. Never look straight at it, not even for a moment, for its light is far too strong for our eyes. And on bright days, its rays can burn our skin, so we cover up, seek the shade, and protect ourselves, and enjoy it safely.

image.note: Children playing safely in the sun, shaded and covered

pages.text: So the next time the Sun rises, remember what it truly is: not a small coin in the sky, but a giant star, our own star, so vast a million earths would fit inside, feeding your world with light and warmth, and turning, quietly, every living thing on earth. All of it, from one steady, blazing star.

image.note: The Sun rising, feeding a whole living world

pages.text: Words to know. Star: a giant ball of burning gas. The Sun: our own star. Solar System: the Sun and its family of planets. Orbit: the great loop a planet makes around the Sun. Season: a time of year caused by the earth's tilt.

image.note: Labelled diagram of the Sun and Solar System

pages.text: The Sun is one star among billions, but it is ours, and our whole world depends on it. Sometimes the most extraordinary thing in the sky is the one we see every single day. What else in your everyday world is more amazing than it looks?

image.note: The everyday Sun, seen with new wonder
